description_full: Winnebago Industries, Inc. manufactures and sells outdoor lifestyle products primarily for use in leisure travel and outdoor recreation activities. It operates through three segments: Towable RV, Motorhome RV, and Marine. The company offers towable products that are non-motorized vehicles to be towed by automobiles, pickup trucks, SUVs, or vans for use as temporary living quarters, such as conventional travel trailers, fifth wheels, folding camper trailers, truck campers, and park models under the Winnebago and Grand Design brand names. It also provides motorhome RV, a self-propelled mobile dwelling used primarily as temporary living quarters during vacation and camping trips, or to support active and mobile lifestyles under the Winnebago, Newmar, and Grand Design brand names. In addition, the company offers battery solutions; other specialty commercial vehicles for law enforcement command centers, mobile medical clinics, and mobile office spaces; and commercial vehicles as bare shells to third-party upfitters, as well as manufactures and sells recreational boats under the Chris-Craft and Barletta brand names. Further, it is involved in the original equipment manufacturing of parts for other manufacturers and commercial vehicles. The company sells its products primarily through independent dealers in the United States, Canada, and internationally. Winnebago Industries, Inc. was incorporated in 1958 and is based in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Winnebago Industries, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $892M market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $145M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.89× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.2×.

Shareholder yield of 4.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.8% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Consumer Cyclical median (8%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.30x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-28.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 28% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 38% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 1.10, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.35 vs 5y 1.16), so read it loosely.
About $16.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 67% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 41% below its DCF fair value of $53.35, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $38.78 to $76.05 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Cyclical peers: cheaper on P/FCF 6.2 vs 16.5, richer on P/E 25.9 vs 19.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 51% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 16.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $35.57 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.62).
It runs a 13% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.89x.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.1x net debt to EBITDA ($181.4M of cash against $443.3M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.4, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -8.2% over 3 years, -5.7% over 5 years and 10.7% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is -1, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 45.3% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.8%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 4.7% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 4.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 116% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 13.2% of the float, 4.5 days to cover.
people: With about 5,000 employees, each generates about $541K of revenue, 1.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 11.6% a year.
That works out to $29K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (5x revenue per employee).
